groups.title: Session Management
groups.question: You are adding login to your Remix app with cookie sessions, but logins sometimes do not stick. Explain how Remix sessions are stored and saved.

followUps.createCookieSessionStorage: What does createCookieSessionStorage do and why does the secret matter?
followUps.commitSession and destroySession: Why might a login not stick after you set the user id in the session?

evidence.text: Session data is stored in a signed cookie.
A strong secret signs it so users cannot change it.
Secrets should be kept private and can be rotated.
Changes only persist when commitSession is called.
Its Set-Cookie header must be returned in the Response.
destroySession clears the session on logout the same way.

notEnough: Only saying you commit the session.

groups.title: Password and User Auth
groups.question: Your user table could leak one day, and attackers might guess which usernames exist by timing login responses. Explain how you would store and check passwords.

followUps.Timing-Safe Comparisons: How can a normal string comparison leak information, and how do you prevent it?

evidence.text: bcrypt is slow and salted on purpose.
A leaked database is then very hard to crack.
Fast hashes like MD5 can be cracked quickly.
A normal comparison stops at the first different character.
Response time differences can reveal information to attackers.
Constant-time comparison functions and consistent login responses prevent this.

groups.title: Cookie Security
groups.question: A security review flags your session cookie settings, and you want a 'Saved!' message after redirecting. Explain cookie attributes and flash messages.

followUps.HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite Attribute: What do HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite do for a session cookie?
followUps.Flash Messages via Session: How do flash messages work in Remix sessions?

evidence.text: HttpOnly stops JavaScript from reading the cookie.
Secure sends it only over HTTPS.
SameSite Lax or Strict blocks most cross-site uses, which helps against CSRF.
A flash value is stored in the session for the next request.
It is removed automatically after being read.
The session must be committed after reading so the value is cleared.

groups.title: OAuth and Third-Party Auth
groups.question: You need GitHub login and must protect actions that other sites might try to trigger. Explain remix-auth and CSRF protection.

followUps.CSRF Protection in Remix Actions: Is SameSite enough to prevent CSRF in Remix?

evidence.text: remix-auth uses strategies for different login methods like OAuth.
It handles redirects, callback verification and saving the user in the session.
This avoids writing error-prone OAuth code by hand.
SameSite cookies give baseline protection.
Endpoints that accept cross-origin requests or older browsers need more.
CSRF tokens or origin checks add protection where needed.
